A1-A2.headline: How Music Recording Changed Over Time

pages.text:
Recording music on separate sound lines keeps every part in time. This idea changed how songs are made.

In 1957, Les Paul bought the first eight-part machine for $10,000. That equals over $114,000 today.
pages.caption: Professional machines used many tracks for music.

imageProvenance.credit: Cliff from I now live in Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Cliff from I now live in Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA (CC BY 2.0)

pages.text:
For many years, only large music rooms could afford these big machines. High prices and strict trade rules kept them out of smaller places.

By the 1960s, famous groups like the Beatles and the Beach Boys used them widely. They mixed voices and music parts to build rich new songs that fans still love.

The 1970s finally brought recording into normal homes. In 1972, TEAC sold the 2340 machine for under $1,000.

Its four sound lines let players try fresh ideas at home without paying for a big music room.
pages.caption: A popular home recorder from 1973.

evidence.articleCaption: The TEAC 2340, a popular early (1973) home multitrack recorder, four tracks on 1⁄4-inch (6.4 mm) tape.

pages.text:
New computer tools later changed music making once again. In 1990, the first computer program for multi-part recording, called Deck, went on sale.

This tool opened the way for Pro Tools in 1991. Soon, music makers moved away from heavy tape machines and began building complete albums on home computers.

B1-B2.headline: The Evolution of Multitrack Recording Technology

pages.text:
Recording separate sounds onto synchronized tracks reshaped modern music production. Artists could refine single parts without replaying whole songs.

In 1957, Les Paul bought the first 8-track machine for $10,000, worth over $114,000 today.
pages.caption: Ampex equipment used in professional recording studios.

imageProvenance.credit: Cliff from I now live in Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Cliff from I now live in Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA (CC BY 2.0)

pages.text:
For several years, these recorders stayed inside large commercial studios because of import rules and steep costs. Most independent musicians could not afford them.

By the 1960s, major acts such as the Beatles and the Beach Boys used them widely. They layered voices and instruments to build rich studio recordings.

The 1970s brought home recording within reach for everyday performers. In 1972, TEAC introduced the 2340, a four-channel recorder priced below $1,000.

Musicians could now experiment freely outside major studios.
pages.caption: The TEAC 2340 brought multitrack recording home.

evidence.articleCaption: The TEAC 2340, a popular early (1973) home multitrack recorder, four tracks on 1⁄4-inch (6.4 mm) tape.

pages.text:
Digital technology later reshaped audio production once again. In 1990, developers released Deck, the first software-based recorder built for personal computers.

That milestone laid the foundation for Pro Tools in 1991. Soon, music recording shifted away from bulky tape machines toward flexible computer software.

C1-C2.headline: Tracing the Technological Trajectory of Multitrack Audio Recording

pages.text:
Isolating discrete acoustic performances across synchronized tracks fundamentally revolutionized contemporary phonographic production.

In 1957, Les Paul acquired the inaugural 8-track apparatus for $10,000, exceeding $114,000 today.
pages.caption: Professional multitrack hardware defined studio capabilities.

imageProvenance.credit: Cliff from I now live in Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Cliff from I now live in Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA (CC BY 2.0)

pages.text:
For years, prohibitive capital expenditures and stringent import regulations restricted multitrack engineering exclusively to institutional recording facilities.

By the 1960s, pioneering ensembles including the Beatles and the Beach Boys harnessed layered overdubbing extensively, elevating studio engineering into an expressive compositional medium.

The 1970s democratized sonic experimentation beyond corporate studios. Released in 1972 below $1,000, the four-channel TEAC 2340 enabled domestic recording.

Independent musicians could iterate freely without institutional patronage.
pages.caption: The TEAC 2340 democratized home multitrack recording.

evidence.articleCaption: The TEAC 2340, a popular early (1973) home multitrack recorder, four tracks on 1⁄4-inch (6.4 mm) tape.

pages.text:
Digital computing subsequently precipitated an even broader paradigm shift across sound engineering. Debuting in 1990, Deck pioneered software-based multitrack recording on desktop architecture.

This architecture catalyzed Pro Tools in 1991, displacing cumbersome analog tape consoles with versatile computational workstations.
